extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and students of comedy/performing arts
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of Rowan Atkinson's comic style
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the characteristics, techniques and career-notes describing Rowan Atkinson's comedic approach — useful for evaluating or emulating his style of comedy in performance or writing. Focuses on his visual/physical comedy, deadpan delivery, character construction and influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/visual comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Best known for his use of physical comedy in his Mr. Bean persona; Atkinson's visually based style, as opposed to his more verbal style, has been compared to Buster Keaton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include solo skits without dialogue (playing an invisible drum kit and an invisible piano) and the Mr. Bean character. Influenced by Jacques Tati and silent-era visual comedians; visual comedy should be deliberate in timing (not under-cranked) and can develop entire comic situations without words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan delivery (especially in authority roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atkinson often plays authority figures (especially priests or vicars) speaking absurd lines with a completely deadpan delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a straight-faced, unflappable persona to heighten absurdity — seen in Blackadder and other roles. The deadpan voice contrasts with the ridiculousness of the content to produce comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acerbic wit and quick put-downs
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing an acerbic wit and armed with numerous quick put-downs (often wasted on those at whom they are directed), e.g. Edmund Blackadder's sarcastic retorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal comedy element: sharp, concise lines and sarcasm that define a character's intelligence and social positioning. Works well in sketch or sitcom contexts where verbal sparring is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction: childlike/selfish protagonist (Mr. Bean)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of Mr Bean is that he's entirely selfish and self-centred and doesn't actually acknowledge the outside world. He's a child in a man's body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building a comic character around a consistent, exaggerated worldview (childlike selfishness) enables visual gags and recurring situational humour; aligns Mr. Bean with visual comedians such as Stan Laurel and Chaplin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switching between visual and verbal modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Atkinson's Mr. Bean persona is visually based, while his other characters rely more on language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comic performers can alternate or blend physical (visual) and verbal comedy depending on character and context — versatility is a strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate pacing and timing in visual comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Jacques Tati's influence: a comic situation can be developed as purely visual and yet it's not under-cranked, it's not speeded-up, it's more deliberate; it takes its time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rushing visual bits; allow gesture and reaction to breathe. Deliberate timing increases clarity and audience appreciation of visual jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment, concentration and control on set
rubrics_metrics.description: On his ability to keep his focus on set during comedic moments, director Oliver Parker noted 'Rowan's focus is astonishing' and that maintaining focus can provoke an 'explosion of laughter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should commit fully to physical actions and maintain concentration so fellow actors and crew can hold back or react appropriately. Strong focus helps land difficult physical or timing-dependent jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantomime/silent-sketch technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Solo skits on television (and without dialogue) have included playing an invisible drum kit and an invisible piano.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pantomime and mime to create universally accessible humour; physical clarity and exaggerated intent are crucial. Works well for international audiences due to low reliance on language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studying and drawing on comedic influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Atkinson's early influences include Beyond the Fringe, Monty Python, John Cleese, Peter Sellers, Barry Humphries, Chaplin, Buster Keaton and Jacques Tati.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning from established comic traditions (satire, sketch, silent-era visual comedy, character work) informs technique and originality. Explicitly referencing influences can shape pacing, character type and gag structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of typecasting and career trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Atkinson has said the Mr. Bean role typecast him to a degree and that highly successful, distinctive roles can both aid and limit a performer's career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating a highly iconic character, weigh immediate popularity against potential long-term typecasting; diversify roles or mediums if avoiding being pigeonholed is a priority.
